tldr: Trained entirely from scratch on robot-native data without relying on internet-video pretraining, the world model DreamFAR achieves 10 FPS real-time operation, long-horizon prediction over one minute, and faithful reproduction of contact physics.
hero_caption: Overview of DreamFAR. It supports real-time teleoperation interaction at 10 Hz, maintains coherence across minutes-long rollouts, and generalizes to over 1,000 diverse tasks.
overview:
World models that take actions as input and predict future visual changes have garnered significant attention as simulators enabling robots to perform complex tasks autonomously. However, existing models face major challenges: they either overfit to a single specific environment, or their predictions rapidly degrade and collapse during long-horizon contact-rich tasks due to compounding errors.

To address this, the authors take an approach distinct from conventional methods that rely on massive web-video pretraining, introducing "DreamFAR," a world model trained from scratch strictly on robot teleoperation data. To prevent object and environment collapse over long horizons, DreamFAR incorporates a "contact-based memory mechanism." The model itself detects "contact events"—moments when the robot makes or breaks contact with an object—stores those critical frames, and retrieves them based on end-effector proximity.

In experiments across 1,000 unseen evaluation episodes, DreamFAR maintained visual quality and geometric consistency significantly superior to existing baselines even under 1-minute long rollouts. Furthermore, policy evaluation conducted within the model showed a strong correlation ($r=0.71$) with real-world task progress, and co-training with human teleoperation data collected entirely inside the model roughly doubled the real-world task success rate.
contributions: Built a 1.9B-parameter world model trained from scratch solely on robot-native data without internet-video pretraining, running in real time at 10 FPS on a commercial GPU.

Enabled long-horizon rollouts that preserve out-of-view object states via a contact-based memory mechanism that self-predicts contact transitions, caches keyframes, and retrieves them by end-effector pose similarity.
Mitigated compounding error accumulation in long autoregressive rollouts by combining unit-sphere latent normalization, a learnable attention sink, and pipelined denoising.

Demonstrated that policy evaluation inside the world model strongly correlates with real-world outcomes ($r=0.71$) and proved that co-training with model-generated demonstrations doubles real-robot performance.

sections.heading: Why Have World Models Struggled with Long-Horizon Contact Tasks?
sections.summary: While world models hold great promise as simulators, error accumulation beyond several tens of seconds and poor generalization to varied contact tasks have been major hurdles. Inspired by human tactile memory, DreamFAR introduces a contact-based memory mechanism to achieve real-time, stable, long-horizon simulation across diverse scenes.
sections.details:
Action-conditioned world models that predict future visual observations are ideal tools for robots to plan actions and simulate outcomes. However, applying existing world models to contact-rich manipulation tasks presents two major roadblocks.

The first is failure in long-horizon rollouts. When rolling out autoregressively for tens of seconds, errors snowball, causing severe image blur and shape degradation. The second is generalizing to contact physics. Because models fail to capture the complex physics of interacting with diverse objects, they struggle in unseen objects and scenes.

To tackle these challenges, the authors propose "DreamFAR." Its core feature is a "contact-based memory mechanism." Much like humans remember the feel of touching something, the model detects the exact moments the robot touches or releases an object (contact transitions) and stores them as keyframes. By keeping track of where an object was placed during past manipulations and recalling that memory whenever the hand approaches, the model preserves object state even when it leaves the field of view. This enables stable predictions spanning multiple minutes while maintaining real-time 10 Hz interaction on a commercial GPU.

sections.heading: From Giant Video Generators to Robot-Native Causal Models
sections.summary: Recent world models typically fine-tune multi-billion-parameter internet-video models on robot data, but they struggle with physical fidelity and long horizons. DreamFAR instead trains causally from scratch purely on robot data, tailoring its memory and caching mechanisms for manipulation.
sections.details:
Research on world models generally branches into two paradigms.

### Video Generation-Based Approaches
The recent mainstream strategy pretrains massive 2B–14B parameter video generation models on web videos and fine-tunes them on robot data. While these models capture rich visual representations, they struggle to reproduce accurate physical dynamics and tend to collapse when generating rollouts longer than their training window. DreamFAR departs from this trend, choosing instead to learn causally (strictly past-to-future) from scratch on robot-native data.

### Causal World Models on Robot Data
Learning world models directly from robot-specific data has a long history. Notable prior works include WEAVER, which trains a causal model on manipulation data, and IWS (Interactive World Simulator), which supports real-time operation. DreamFAR belongs to this lineage but sets itself apart in how it handles long-term memory and physical contacts.

### Long-Horizon Rollouts and Memory Differentiation
Preventing long-horizon failure in video generation requires both an error-mitigating generation process and strategic conditioning on what to remember. Prior works sampled frames based on camera positions or fixed time intervals. DreamFAR instead triggers keyframe storage using model-predicted contact transitions and retrieves them based on end-effector proximity. Additionally, it incorporates a learnable attention sink to retain the initial frame and a rolling KV cache to support streaming generation with constant compute overhead.

sections.heading: Streaming Prediction via Contact Memory and a Unit-Sphere Tokenizer
sections.summary: DreamFAR comprises a visual tokenizer and a dynamics transformer. It achieves collapse-free 10 Hz streaming prediction by combining self-predicted contact-transition memory, unit-sphere latent normalization, and pipelined denoising that hides latency.
sections.details:
Here is how future observations are autoregressively predicted from current observations $\mathbf{x}_t$ and robot actions $\mathbf{a}_t$.

### 3.1 Contact-Based Memory Mechanism
Relying solely on recent frames causes the model to forget where an object was placed once it moves out of view. DreamFAR solves this by pairing a short-term context of the most recent $T$ frames with a long-term memory $\mathcal{M}_t$.

The trigger for writing to memory is a change in contact state. An auxiliary head attached to the transformer predicts binary contact flags $\hat{\mathbf{c}}_t \in \{0, 1\}^2$ for both arms, recording a keyframe whenever a flag flips (an object is grasped or released). This requires no external sensors or manual annotations; it updates entirely through the model's own predictions. For retrieval, frames with high end-effector pose similarity (computed via forward kinematics) to the current hand pose are fetched, fitting into a fixed context budget of 8 frames.

### 3.2 Streaming Dynamics Transformer
The core dynamics model is a 1.9B-parameter transformer. It blends spatial attention within frames and temporal attention across time, employing spatiotemporal attention in select layers to capture complex motion. Moreover, a dedicated learnable sink frame is permanently retained in memory, providing a stable target for attention even when the memory buffer is empty.

To enable real-time 10 Hz inference, DreamFAR pipelines $P=16$ frames at different noise levels in parallel, updating a rolling KV cache while denoising frames step by step. This keeps per-step computation constant regardless of rollout duration.

### 3.3 Unit-Sphere Tokenizer
Long autoregressive rollouts often suffer from scale drift, where latent feature norms gradually blow up. DreamFAR prevents this by applying unit-sphere normalization to the encoder's latent tokens, enforcing an L2 norm of 1 at every spatial position. The decoder uses flow matching, reconstructing high-quality $256 \times 256$ images from Gaussian noise in just 2 Euler integration steps (~14 ms per view).

sections.heading: Impressive 1-Minute Rollouts: Visual Quality, Stability, and Practical Utility
sections.summary: In 1-minute long-horizon rollouts on the public ABC benchmark, DreamFAR substantially outperformed baselines (Cosmos-Predict 2.5, WEAVER, IWS) in visual quality and stability. It also proved effective as a policy evaluation simulator and improved real-world policy performance via co-training.
sections.details:
### 4.1 Experimental Setup
The dataset was collected on a dual-arm YAM robot equipped with 3 cameras. For fair comparison with baselines, models were also evaluated on the public ABC dataset (~131k episodes, ~3,500 hours, 201 tasks), testing across 1,000 unseen evaluation episodes. DreamFAR has 1.9B parameters, compared to ~800M for WEAVER and ~400M for Cosmos-Predict 2.5 and IWS.

### 4.2 Qualitative Results
Across 30-second rollouts involving Lego assembly, manipulating tools and containers (bags, bread, plates), and handling deformable items like skirts, DreamFAR consistently preserved object identity and arm-contact physics. It generalized reliably even to out-of-distribution (OOD) tasks unseen in training.

### 4.3 Long-Horizon Baseline Comparison
During 60-second autonomous rollouts, IWS blurred and collapsed within 10 seconds, WEAVER developed heavy visual hallucinations in the wrist camera views, and Cosmos-Predict 2.5 suffered from drifting arm shapes and textures. DreamFAR generated clean rollouts through the full minute, faithfully maintaining delicate contact tasks such as whiteboard writing. It achieved an average PSNR of 16.4 dB, surpassing Cosmos-Predict 2.5 (15.8 dB), WEAVER (14.5 dB), and IWS (11.0 dB). On FID measuring perceptual quality, while baselines deteriorated past 70 to over 180, DreamFAR rose only mildly from 15 to 32.

### 4.4 Policy Evaluation Application
Policies ($\pi_0$) were executed inside DreamFAR instead of on real robots to evaluate task progress. Across three tasks—putting a plate in a box, tossing a bottle, and folding a T-shirt—progress inside the simulator showed a strong Pearson correlation of $r=0.71$ with real-world executions. While the simulator tended to be slightly optimistic (reaching completion faster), it accurately preserved the relative performance ranking among policies.

### 4.5 Policy Co-Training with Model-Generated Demonstrations
Because DreamFAR runs at 10 Hz in real time, human operators can collect teleoperated demonstrations directly inside the model using leader arms. Adding 75 model-generated demonstrations to 75 real-robot demonstrations doubled the real-world success rate on a chip-bag-to-basket task, reaching 63%.

### 4.6 Contact Memory Ablation
On a task requiring objects to be organized into a box, the proposed contact-based memory was compared against no memory and a fixed 1-second sparse memory. Without memory, the contents of the box vanished once out of view; with sparse memory, completely different objects were hallucinated. Storing keyframes at contact transitions and retrieving them by end-effector pose proved essential to maintaining accurate object arrangements.

sections.heading: Discussion and Limitations: Toward General Simulators Beyond a Single Station
sections.summary: DreamFAR achieves real-time, long-horizon manipulation simulation using contact-based memory and an efficient causal design. Current limitations include reliance on a specific workstation setup, restriction to a single embodiment, and dexterity bounded by parallel grippers.
sections.details:
DreamFAR highlights the viability of practical world models that can simulate contact-heavy robot tasks in real time over extended horizons. Its potential utility in robotics research is wide-ranging, from offline policy verification to data collection for boosting real-world performance.

Nonetheless, several limitations remain:

- Scene diversity: Experiments were conducted within a dedicated workstation (YAM setup); expanding to open-world scenes with shifting backgrounds and lighting is an essential next step.
- Robot embodiment: The system was developed for a single robot configuration; adapting to diverse multi-robot setups with different degrees of freedom and kinematics is left to future work.
- End-effector dexterity: The setup relies on parallel-jaw grippers. Modeling finer contact interactions, such as multi-fingered in-hand reorientation, requires further exploration.

sections.heading: Appendix: Tokenizer Details and the Contact Labeling Pipeline
sections.summary: The tokenizer compresses 3 views into 192 tokens per frame, regularized by unit-sphere normalization and a uniformity loss. The contact prediction head is supervised using an automated labeling pipeline powered by a vision-language model (VLM).
sections.details:
Key implementation and training details from the appendix are summarized below.

### Tokenizer Architecture and Normalization
At each timestep, 3 camera views ($256 \times 256$ RGB) are mapped by a convolutional encoder into $16 \times 16$ spatial grids of 16-dimensional latent representations. Latent vectors at each position are strictly normalized to have an L2 norm of 1 on the unit sphere before being reconstructed by the flow decoder. The training objective combines flow matching loss, perceptual loss (LPIPS), a feature alignment loss against a pretrained ViT, and a uniformity loss that prevents latent space collapse.

### Contact Labeler Construction
Supervision for the auxiliary contact head is generated by a fine-tuned vision-language model (VLM). The VLM processes 8-frame clips combining base and wrist camera perspectives to predict contact probabilities, which are then smoothed using a box filter and hysteresis thresholding (triggering contact above 0.6 and release below 0.4). Relying solely on gripper open/close states failed to capture non-prehensile contacts like pushing and missed roughly 60% of real grasps, making this visual VLM labeler critical.

takeaways: High-fidelity, collapse-free world models can be trained without internet-video pretraining by building a causal architecture specialized for robot-native data.
Preserving the state of out-of-view objects is best achieved by updating and querying memory based on physical contact make/break events rather than fixed temporal sampling.
Rollout progress within the world model strongly correlates with real-world execution, and teleoperation data collected entirely inside the model can double real-robot policy success.
limitations: Evaluations are restricted to a specific workstation setup (the YAM environment), leaving generalization to open-world environments with varying lighting and backgrounds untested.
The model is tailored to a single dual-arm setup with parallel grippers, making direct application to multi-fingered hands or different robot kinematics challenging.
Although policy progress inside the simulator strongly correlates with real-world execution, the simulator tends to produce slightly optimistic evaluations compared to real runs.
